flashcards.front: Public vs. private vs. hybrid vs. community cloud
flashcards.back: Public: shared infrastructure owned by a third-party provider. Private: dedicated to one organization, on-premises or hosted. Hybrid: a mix of both, often connected for workload portability. Community: shared by several organizations with common requirements, like agencies in the same industry.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: "hybrid" specifically implies connected, coordinated environments — just using two unrelated clouds for different things is closer to multi-cloud, not hybrid.

flashcards.back: Scalability is the general capacity to handle more (or less) load by adding or removing resources, which can be planned and manual. Elasticity is scaling that happens automatically and dynamically in response to real-time demand.
flashcards.detail: Every elastic system is scalable, but not every scalable system is elastic — a system that only scales through a change request ticket is scalable, not elastic.

flashcards.back: Vertical scaling ("scaling up") adds resources — CPU, RAM — to an existing instance. Horizontal scaling ("scaling out") adds more instances running in parallel.
flashcards.detail: Vertical scaling usually requires a restart and has a hardware ceiling. Horizontal scaling avoids both, but requires the workload to be designed to run across multiple instances (e.g., stateless, load-balanced).

flashcards.front: High availability vs. fault tolerance vs. disaster recovery
flashcards.back: High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy, but a brief failover interruption may still occur. Fault tolerance keeps the system running through a failure with no interruption at all, usually at higher cost. Disaster recovery is the plan and process for restoring service after a major outage that HA/fault tolerance didn't prevent.
flashcards.detail: HA and fault tolerance are about avoiding downtime; DR assumes downtime already happened and is about getting back up.

flashcards.back: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after an outage. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as time since the last good backup.
flashcards.detail: A 4-hour RPO means backups need to run at least every 4 hours. RTO and RPO are set by business requirements first, then the backup/DR architecture is built to meet them — not the other way around.

flashcards.front: Block vs. file vs. object storage
flashcards.back: Block storage presents raw, low-latency volumes ideal for databases and VM disks. File storage presents a shared, hierarchical filesystem accessed over a protocol like NFS or SMB. Object storage holds data as flat, metadata-rich objects, built for massive scale rather than low-latency random access.
flashcards.detail: A relational database wants block storage. A shared team drive wants file storage. Millions of backup archives or media files want object storage.

flashcards.back: Round robin cycles requests evenly across servers in order. Least connections sends new requests to whichever server currently has the fewest active connections. Weighted (round robin or least connections) accounts for servers with different capacities. Source/IP-affinity keeps a given client pinned to the same backend server.
flashcards.detail: Source affinity matters for stateful apps that keep session data on one server — losing that pinning mid-session can log a user out or break their session.

flashcards.back: Authentication verifies who you are. Authorization determines what you're allowed to do once verified. Accounting logs what was actually done, for audit purposes.
flashcards.detail: A stolen-but-valid password is an authentication success with an authorization failure waiting to happen — the identity checks out, but it isn't really that person acting.

flashcards.back: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions based on a user's assigned role (e.g., "Backup Operator"). Attribute-based access control (ABAC) evaluates a combination of attributes at request time — user department, resource tag, time of day, location — to make a more granular decision.
flashcards.detail: RBAC is simpler to administer at scale; ABAC is more flexible but harder to audit because the effective rule set is computed dynamically rather than assigned directly.

flashcards.front: Encryption at rest vs. in transit vs. in use
flashcards.back: At rest protects stored data (on disk). In transit protects data moving across a network (e.g., TLS). In use protects data while it's actively being processed in memory, which is the hardest of the three to achieve and typically needs specialized hardware (e.g., a trusted execution environment).
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap: encrypting a database at rest does nothing to protect a query result being sent to a client over an unencrypted connection — that needs in-transit encryption too.

flashcards.back: A security model that never grants trust based on network location alone. Every request is independently verified — identity, device posture, and context — regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the traditional network perimeter.
flashcards.detail: Zero Trust means a compromised perimeter (e.g., a stolen VPN credential) still isn't enough on its own to reach sensitive resources, because every subsequent request is re-checked.

flashcards.back: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors traffic and alerts on suspicious activity, but doesn't block it. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) sits inline and can actively block or drop traffic it identifies as malicious.
flashcards.detail: IPS's ability to block traffic is also its biggest risk: a false positive can actively break legitimate traffic, which a passive IDS never would.

flashcards.back: A stateful firewall tracks the state of active connections and automatically allows return traffic for a connection it already approved. A stateless filter (like a basic ACL) evaluates every packet independently against its rule set, with no memory of prior traffic.
flashcards.detail: Stateless filtering needs explicit rules for both inbound and outbound halves of a connection, since it has no concept of "this reply belongs to a request I already allowed."

flashcards.back: Tokenization replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive substitute (a token) that has no mathematical relationship to the original value, with the real data stored separately in a vault. Encryption transforms data using a reversible mathematical algorithm and a key.
flashcards.detail: Because a token can't be mathematically reversed back to the original value even if you had unlimited computing power, tokenization is often preferred for things like stored payment card numbers.

flashcards.back: Blue-green runs two full, identical production environments; traffic is switched entirely from one to the other once the new version is verified. Canary releases the new version to a small subset of users/traffic first, gradually increasing exposure as confidence grows.
flashcards.detail: Blue-green gives an instant, all-or-nothing rollback (just switch traffic back). Canary limits the blast radius of a bad release but takes longer to fully roll out.

flashcards.back: A rolling deployment updates instances gradually, a few at a time, so the service stays available throughout. An in-place deployment updates a server directly, typically taking that instance offline (or degraded) during the update.
flashcards.detail: Rolling deployments need a load balancer removing an instance from rotation before updating it, then adding it back — skip that step and you're serving errors from a mid-update instance.

flashcards.front: Full vs. incremental vs. differential backup
flashcards.back: A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind (fastest to create, slowest to restore — needs the full plus every incremental since). A differential backup copies everything changed since the last full backup (restore needs only the full plus the latest differential).
flashcards.detail: Incremental backups are smaller and faster individually, but a restore has to replay every incremental in sequence — if one link in that chain is corrupt, the restore fails past that point.

flashcards.front: P2V, V2V, P2C, and V2C migrations
flashcards.back: P2V converts a physical server into a virtual machine. V2V moves a VM from one hypervisor/platform to another. P2C moves a still-physical on-premises workload straight into the cloud. V2C moves a workload that is already virtualized on-premises into the cloud — the distinction is what state the source was in before the move, not just where it ends up.
flashcards.detail: A 'lift and shift' cloud migration is usually a P2C or V2C migration — moving the workload largely as-is, versus refactoring it to use cloud-native PaaS services instead.

flashcards.back: Thick provisioning allocates the full requested storage capacity immediately, whether or not it's used. Thin provisioning allocates storage on demand as data is actually written, letting you over-commit total capacity across multiple volumes.
flashcards.detail: Thin provisioning's risk: if many thin-provisioned volumes are all filled close to their allocated limit at once, the underlying physical storage can run out even though each individual volume still shows free space.

flashcards.back: Defining infrastructure — networks, VMs, storage — as declarative configuration files that can be version-controlled and used to deploy the same environment repeatably, instead of manual configuration.
flashcards.detail: IaC's real value in a cert-exam sense: it makes environments idempotent and auditable — you can always tell exactly what was deployed by reading the file, and redeploying it produces the same result.

flashcards.front: Continuous integration vs. continuous delivery vs. continuous deployment
flashcards.back: Continuous integration merges code changes and runs automated tests frequently. Continuous delivery goes further, keeping code always in a releasable state after passing tests, but a human still approves the actual release. Continuous deployment removes that manual gate — every change that passes automated tests ships to production automatically.
flashcards.detail: The one-word difference between 'delivery' and 'deployment' is the whole distinction: delivery is release-ready, deployment is already released.

flashcards.back: Automation handles a single, well-defined task without human intervention (e.g., auto-restarting a failed service). Orchestration coordinates multiple automated tasks together into a larger workflow (e.g., provisioning a VM, then configuring it, then registering it with a load balancer, in sequence).
flashcards.detail: Orchestration is built ON TOP OF automation — you can't orchestrate a workflow out of steps that aren't individually automated first.

flashcards.back: Chargeback actually bills internal departments for their share of cloud costs, moving real budget between them. Showback reports each department's usage and cost for visibility and accountability, without an actual internal transfer of funds.
flashcards.detail: Showback is often adopted first, as a lower-friction way to build cost awareness before an organization is ready for the accounting complexity of real chargeback.

flashcards.back: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is used to monitor and manage network devices, polling or receiving traps about their status and metrics. Syslog is a standard for forwarding log messages from a device or application to a centralized logging server.
flashcards.detail: SNMP is generally for structured, device-health metrics (interface status, CPU load); syslog is for free-form event and log messages — the two are often run side by side, not as alternatives to each other.

flashcards.back: A baseline is the normal, expected range of a metric under typical conditions, established by observing it over time. A threshold is a specific value that, when crossed, triggers an alert or action.
flashcards.detail: Thresholds set without first establishing a baseline tend to be either too sensitive (constant false alarms) or too loose (real problems go unnoticed) — baselining comes first.

flashcards.back: A Service Level Agreement typically defines measurable commitments like uptime percentage, response time to incidents, and resolution time — along with the penalties or credits owed if those commitments aren't met.
flashcards.detail: "Five nines" (99.999% uptime) allows only about 5 minutes of downtime a year — a useful number to recognize on the exam when a scenario states an uptime percentage and asks how much downtime it allows.

flashcards.back: A centralized repository that tracks an organization's IT assets (configuration items) and the relationships between them — which servers depend on which services, who owns what, and so on.
flashcards.detail: A CMDB is what lets a change or incident process answer "what else does this affect?" instead of relying on institutional memory.

flashcards.back: A pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more tightly-coupled containers that share networking and storage. A node is a physical or virtual machine that runs pods. A cluster is the full set of nodes managed together, coordinated by a control plane.
flashcards.detail: Scaling in Kubernetes usually means adding more pod replicas (horizontal), not making one pod bigger — matching the general cloud preference for horizontal over vertical scaling.

flashcards.back: 1) Identify the problem. 2) Establish a theory of probable cause. 3) Test the theory. 4) Establish a plan of action and implement the solution. 5) Verify full system functionality. 6) Document findings and outcomes.
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap: jumping straight to "implement a solution" without first testing the theory — a plausible-sounding cause that turns out to be wrong wastes a maintenance window and can make things worse.

flashcards.back: In a multi-tenant environment, one tenant's heavy resource usage (CPU, disk I/O, network) degrades performance for other tenants sharing the same underlying physical hardware.
flashcards.detail: The typical fix is resource governance — CPU/IO limits, quality-of-service policies, or moving the noisy workload to dedicated hardware — rather than something the affected tenant can usually fix from their own side.

flashcards.back: Cloud resources — disks, snapshots, public IPs, load balancers — left behind after the workload that created them was deleted, but never cleaned up themselves. They keep incurring cost with no one using them.
flashcards.detail: A classic root cause of 'why is our bill higher than expected' when the deployed workload footprint hasn't obviously grown.

flashcards.back: A failure where the network path and destination service are both healthy, but a hostname simply won't resolve to the correct IP address — often due to a misconfigured or stale DNS record, or a caching resolver serving an outdated answer.
flashcards.detail: A good diagnostic instinct: if a service is unreachable by name but reachable by its raw IP address, the problem is DNS, not the network path or the service itself.

flashcards.back: Latency is the delay before data begins to transfer (how long a single round trip takes). Bandwidth is the total volume of data that can transfer per unit of time once it's flowing. A connection can have plenty of bandwidth and still feel slow due to high latency.
flashcards.detail: A common trap: adding more bandwidth to a connection does nothing to fix a latency problem — they're independent characteristics with different causes and different fixes. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a latency fix specifically, not a bandwidth one.

flashcards.back: A failure where infrastructure and configuration are otherwise correct, but a service stops working (or refuses to scale further) because a software license has expired or a licensed capacity limit (e.g., number of cores or seats) has been reached.
flashcards.detail: Easy to overlook because nothing about the infrastructure itself changed — the exam likes scenarios where a service 'just stopped working' with no recent configuration change, pointing at licensing or a certificate expiration instead.

flashcards.front: Root cause analysis vs. a workaround
flashcards.back: A workaround restores service quickly without necessarily fixing the underlying issue (e.g., restarting a hung service). Root cause analysis identifies and addresses the actual reason the problem happened, to prevent recurrence.
flashcards.detail: Applying a workaround isn't a mistake under time pressure — the mistake is stopping there and never following up with root cause analysis, so the same incident quietly repeats.

flashcards.back: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) provides raw compute, storage, and networking — the customer manages the OS upward. PaaS (Platform as a Service) adds a managed runtime/OS layer so the customer just deploys code. SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers a complete, ready-to-use application, with the provider managing everything underneath.
flashcards.detail: The customer's management responsibility shrinks as you move IaaS -> PaaS -> SaaS: with IaaS you patch the OS yourself, with SaaS you manage nothing but your own data and user accounts.

flashcards.back: A virtual machine virtualizes hardware and includes its own full guest operating system, managed by a hypervisor. A container virtualizes at the OS level, packaging an application with its dependencies but sharing the host's kernel — no separate guest OS per instance.
flashcards.detail: That shared kernel is why containers start in seconds (or less) and have a much smaller footprint than a VM, but it also means containers on the same host are less isolated from each other than separate VMs would be.

flashcards.back: MFA combines at least two of: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a hardware token or authenticator app), something you are (a biometric like a fingerprint), and sometimes somewhere you are (location) or something you do (behavioral).
flashcards.detail: Two passwords, or a password plus a security question, are both still just "something you know" twice — that's not true multifactor, even though it feels like an extra step.

flashcards.back: PKI issues and manages digital certificates that bind a public key to an identity, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). TLS uses this to let a client verify a server's identity and negotiate encrypted communication.
flashcards.detail: A certificate that has expired, or was issued by a CA the client doesn't trust, will fail validation even if the underlying network path and server are perfectly healthy — a common troubleshooting trap that looks like a network outage but isn't.

flashcards.back: Patch management is the process of testing, approving, and applying software/OS updates on a controlled schedule rather than ad hoc. A maintenance window is a pre-approved, communicated time slot during which changes (including patching) are allowed to cause disruption.
flashcards.detail: Testing a patch in staging before production, and scheduling the rollout in an approved window, are both change management applied specifically to patching.

flashcards.back: Using historical usage trends and baselines to forecast future resource needs (storage, compute, bandwidth) and provision ahead of demand, rather than reacting after a resource is already exhausted.
flashcards.detail: Good capacity planning depends on having a solid baseline first — without knowing normal growth trends, it's just guessing.

flashcards.front: Hot, warm, and cold DR sites
flashcards.back: A hot site is fully equipped and kept in near real-time sync with production, ready for near-instant failover (fastest, most expensive). A warm site has infrastructure in place but needs some setup/data sync before use. A cold site has only basic facilities (power, space) and needs full buildout and data restoration before use (slowest, cheapest).
flashcards.detail: Site choice is really an RTO/cost trade-off: a lower RTO requirement pushes toward a hot site, while a looser RTO can tolerate the savings of a cold site.

flashcards.back: RAID 0 stripes data across disks for performance with no redundancy (one disk failure loses everything). RAID 1 mirrors data for redundancy with no capacity gain. RAID 5 stripes data plus distributed parity, tolerating one disk failure. RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping for both redundancy and performance, at the cost of half the raw capacity.
flashcards.detail: RAID 0 is sometimes mistaken for a resilience feature because it "spreads" data across disks — it actually has zero fault tolerance and is only about speed.

flashcards.back: A geographically distributed set of edge servers that cache content closer to end users, reducing the round-trip distance data has to travel and offloading traffic from the origin server.
flashcards.detail: A CDN mainly helps with latency and origin load, not raw available bandwidth — recognizing which one a scenario is actually describing (see latency vs. bandwidth problems) decides whether a CDN is really the fix.

flashcards.back: A formal, documented process for proposing, reviewing, approving, and recording a change to production systems, including a rollback plan, before the change is actually made.
flashcards.detail: A configuration management database (CMDB) is what change management updates once a change is approved and completed — the CMDB should always reflect the environment's true current state.

flashcards.back: A documented, step-by-step procedure for a specific operational task or incident response, written so it can be followed consistently by different people (or triggered automatically) with the same result each time.
flashcards.detail: A runbook is what automation vs. orchestration tooling actually executes — the runbook is the procedure; automation/orchestration is what carries it out without a human doing each step by hand.

flashcards.back: A periodic probe the load balancer sends to each backend instance to confirm it's actually able to serve traffic — an instance that fails enough consecutive checks is automatically taken out of rotation until it passes again.
flashcards.detail: This is what makes load balancing algorithms actually resilient to a failed instance — the algorithm only ever picks among instances the health check currently considers healthy.

flashcards.back: A cloud-delivered, centrally managed firewall service applied across an environment without deploying and maintaining physical or virtual firewall appliances at every location.
flashcards.detail: FWaaS commonly layers both stateful vs. stateless packet filtering and IDS vs. IPS-style inspection into one managed service rather than stitching those together from separate appliances.

flashcards.back: A dedicated infrastructure layer (typically sidecar proxies alongside each service) that handles service-to-service traffic concerns — routing, retries, encryption, observability — without every microservice implementing that logic itself.
flashcards.detail: In a Kubernetes: pod, node, and cluster environment, a service mesh's sidecar proxies are commonly injected into each pod, working alongside the containers rather than replacing them.

flashcards.back: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the physical hardware with no host OS underneath it — the standard for production datacenters and cloud providers. A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on top of a regular host OS, more common for a desktop/test environment.
flashcards.detail: Removing the host OS layer is exactly why Type 1 has less overhead and better performance — there's one less layer between the VM and the physical hardware than in a P2V, V2V, P2C, and V2C migrations scenario running Type 2.

flashcards.back: Lets a user authenticate once and gain access to multiple independent systems without signing in separately to each one, using a shared trust relationship between the identity provider and each application.
flashcards.detail: SSO is squarely about the authentication piece of authentication vs. authorization vs. accounting (AAA) — it doesn't decide what a user can do once signed in, only that they don't have to prove who they are over and over.

flashcards.back: A deployment approach where servers or containers are never modified after being provisioned — a change means replacing the instance entirely with a newly built one, rather than patching a live system in place.
flashcards.detail: This pairs naturally with Infrastructure as Code (IaC): if the whole environment is defined in code, replacing an instance instead of patching it becomes cheap and repeatable rather than risky.

flashcards.back: Deliberately injecting failures into a production or production-like system (killing an instance, adding latency, cutting a dependency) to verify that resilience mechanisms actually work as designed, instead of only assuming they do.
flashcards.detail: This is how a team actually validates the high availability vs. fault tolerance vs. disaster recovery claims made about a system, rather than discovering the gaps for the first time during a real outage.

questions.question: A university, a research lab, and a hospital network in the same region want to jointly fund and share a cloud environment built specifically around their shared compliance needs, without opening it to the general public. Which deployment model is this?
options: Community cloud
Public cloud
Hybrid cloud
Private cloud, shared under a joint support contract
questions.explanation: Community cloud is shared by several organizations with common requirements or compliance needs, distinct from a public cloud (open to anyone) or a private cloud (dedicated to one organization, even under a shared contract). Hybrid specifically means a mix of private and public environments connected together, which isn't what's described here.

questions.question: An application automatically adds server instances at 9 AM on weekdays and removes them at 6 PM, based on a fixed calendar schedule rather than real-time load. Which best describes this behavior?
options: Vertical scaling, since existing servers were resized rather than any new ones added
Scheduled scaling, a form of scalability but not elasticity
Elasticity, since it happens without manual intervention
Fault tolerance, since the system keeps running without any interruption during the schedule change
questions.explanation: This is automatic, but it's reacting to a fixed schedule, not real-time demand — elasticity specifically means scaling dynamically in response to actual, current load. It's also adding whole instances (horizontal), not resizing an existing one (vertical), and has nothing to do with tolerating failures.

questions.question: A database server is running out of headroom under load, and the team's fix is to increase its allocated vCPUs and RAM. Which approach does this represent, and what is its main limitation?
options: Horizontal scaling — it's limited by the load balancer's connection limit
Vertical scaling — it's limited by the maximum size of a single instance and typically requires a restart
Elasticity — it's limited by the auto-scaling group's minimum instance count
Fault tolerance — it's limited by the number of availability zones in the region
questions.explanation: Resizing a single existing instance is vertical scaling (scaling up), which is capped by the largest instance size available and usually needs a reboot to apply. Horizontal scaling would mean adding more instances rather than resizing one, which isn't what happened here.

questions.question: A business states its recovery point objective (RPO) for a critical system as 15 minutes. What does this actually commit the organization to?
options: Notifying customers of an outage within 15 minutes
Backing up or replicating that system's data at least every 15 minutes
Restoring the system within 15 minutes of an outage being declared
Completing a full system failover within 15 minutes
questions.explanation: RPO is about acceptable data loss, measured in time — a 15-minute RPO means the data backup/replication cadence must be frequent enough that no more than 15 minutes of data could ever be lost. Committing to a restoration or failover time window is what RTO covers instead.

questions.question: A media company needs to store several petabytes of archived video files that are rarely modified once uploaded, accessed by a web application via simple HTTP requests rather than a mounted filesystem. Which storage type fits best?
options: Block storage
A relational database
File storage
Object storage
questions.explanation: Object storage is built for exactly this: massive scale, HTTP-based access, metadata-rich, rarely-modified files. Block storage is meant for low-latency random I/O like a database's own disk, and file storage implies a mounted, hierarchical filesystem — neither matches 'accessed via HTTP requests, not a mounted drive.'

questions.question: A stateful web application keeps each logged-in user's session data cached only on the specific backend server that first handled their login. Which load balancing approach is required to keep that application working correctly across multiple servers?
options: Weighted round robin based on server capacity
Round robin
Source/IP affinity (sticky sessions)
Least connections
questions.explanation: Since session data lives only on one specific server, that same client must keep being routed back to it — which is exactly what source/IP affinity provides. Round robin, least connections, and weighted round robin all distribute requests based on load or order, with no guarantee a given client lands back on the same server twice.

questions.question: A company wants a CDN (content delivery network) primarily to improve which aspect of serving static website content to a global audience?
options: Encryption of data at rest
Latency, by caching content at edge locations closer to each user
Identity and access management for the origin server
The RPO of the origin server's backups
questions.explanation: A CDN's core purpose is caching content at edge locations near end users, cutting the round-trip distance and thus latency. It doesn't handle at-rest encryption, IAM, or backup objectives — those are separate concerns entirely.

questions.question: A user's password is stolen and used to log into a system successfully. Security logs show the attacker's every action was later traced and reviewed in detail. Which part of AAA specifically enabled that after-the-fact review?
options: Authentication
Authorization
Non-repudiation
Accounting
questions.explanation: Accounting is the logging of what was actually done, which is what allowed the after-the-fact review. Authentication (verifying identity) actually succeeded here despite being a stolen credential, and authorization determines what actions are permitted — neither one is about producing a reviewable log.

questions.question: A company wants access decisions that factor in the requesting user's department, the sensitivity tag on the specific resource, and the time of day — evaluated dynamically for each request rather than through a fixed set of assigned roles. Which access control model fits?
options: Discretionary access control granted permanently at account creation
RBAC (role-based access control)
ABAC (attribute-based access control)
Mandatory access control based on system-assigned classification labels
questions.explanation: ABAC evaluates multiple attributes — department, resource tags, time of day — dynamically at request time. RBAC instead grants a fixed set of permissions tied to an assigned role, which doesn't flex per-request based on multiple contextual attributes.

questions.question: A database is fully encrypted on disk, but a recent incident involved an attacker intercepting query results as they traveled from the database server to a reporting application over an internal network. What security gap does this specifically point to?
options: Missing encryption at rest
Missing role-based access control on the reporting application
Missing multifactor authentication on the database
Missing encryption in transit
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data sitting on disk, which was already in place — it does nothing for data moving across the network afterward. The interception happened in transit, so that's the specific gap, not MFA or RBAC, which govern who can log in and what they can do, not how data is protected while moving.

questions.question: A security appliance sits inline with network traffic and is configured to automatically drop packets that match a known attack signature, without waiting for a human to respond. Which type of system is this?
options: A vulnerability scanner
An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System)
A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform
An IDS (Intrusion Detection System)
questions.explanation: Actively blocking traffic inline is the defining feature of an IPS. An IDS would only alert without blocking, a vulnerability scanner looks for weaknesses rather than live traffic, and a SIEM aggregates and correlates security events rather than acting on individual packets itself.

questions.question: A network engineer configures a set of packet filtering rules that evaluate every single packet independently against a static rule list, with no awareness of whether a packet belongs to a connection already allowed. What kind of filtering is this, and what does it require that a connection-aware alternative would not?
options: Stateless filtering — it requires explicit rules for both directions of every allowed connection
Stateful filtering — it requires explicit rules for both directions of every allowed connection
Stateless filtering — it automatically permits return traffic for any connection it already approved
An IPS — it requires a signature database to be kept current
questions.explanation: No memory of prior traffic is exactly what makes it stateless, and because it can't recognize 'this is a reply to something I already let through,' both the outbound request and the inbound reply need their own explicit rule. A stateful filter is what automatically permits that return traffic without a second rule.

questions.question: A company stores customer credit card numbers by substituting each one with a randomly generated, unrelated value, keeping the real numbers in a separate secure vault. Even with unlimited computing power, the substitute values cannot be mathematically reversed to reveal the originals. Which technique is this?
options: Symmetric encryption
Tokenization
Asymmetric encryption
Hashing with a fixed salt
questions.explanation: The key detail is 'no mathematical relationship' and 'cannot be reversed even with unlimited computing power' — that rules out encryption entirely (which is always reversible given the right key) and describes tokenization instead, where the substitute has no computable link back to the original at all.

questions.question: An organization adopts a Zero Trust approach after a VPN credential is stolen and used to connect to the internal network. Which outcome would Zero Trust have most directly prevented?
options: The attacker being detected by an IDS
The attacker reaching sensitive internal resources on the strength of network access alone, without further verification
The need for any authentication at all once inside the network perimeter
The VPN credential being stolen in the first place
questions.explanation: Zero Trust's core principle is never granting trust based on network location alone — so reaching the internal network wouldn't be enough on its own to reach sensitive resources, since every subsequent request is independently verified. It doesn't prevent credential theft itself, and it actually requires MORE verification once inside, not less.

questions.question: A team maintains two complete, identical production environments. New releases go to the currently-idle one, get fully verified, and then all live traffic is switched over to it at once — with the old environment kept running briefly in case an instant rollback is needed. Which deployment strategy is this?
options: Blue-green deployment
Rolling deployment
Canary deployment
In-place deployment
questions.explanation: Maintaining two full, identical environments and switching all traffic over at once is the defining trait of blue-green. Canary would gradually shift a small slice of traffic instead of switching all at once, and rolling/in-place deployments update the existing environment directly rather than maintaining a full duplicate.

questions.question: A company runs a full backup every Sunday and a differential backup every other day of the week. If a failure happens on Thursday, which backups are needed to fully restore the data, and in what order?
options: Sunday's full backup, then every differential from Monday through Wednesday, in sequence
Sunday's full backup, then Thursday's differential backup
Only Wednesday's differential backup
Sunday's full backup, then Wednesday's differential backup
questions.explanation: A differential backup captures everything changed since the last FULL backup, so the most recent differential (Wednesday's) already contains all of Monday through Wednesday's changes on its own — only the full plus that single latest differential are needed. Needing to replay every differential in sequence is the restore pattern for incremental backups, not differential.

questions.question: A company is moving a workload from an on-premises physical server directly into a cloud provider's virtual machine service, largely unchanged. What type of migration is this?
options: V2C (virtual-to-cloud)
V2V (virtual-to-virtual)
P2V only, with no cloud component
P2C (physical-to-cloud)
questions.explanation: Starting from a physical server and ending in the cloud makes this P2C. V2V would apply if the source were already a VM being moved to a different hypervisor, and V2C would apply if the source were already virtualized on-premises before the cloud move — neither matches a physical starting point.

questions.question: A storage administrator allocates 500 GB volumes to twenty different servers on a storage array that only physically has 3 TB of actual capacity, on the assumption that most volumes won't use their full allocation at once. Which approach is this, and what is its main risk?
options: Thin provisioning — the array reserves the full 500 GB physically before any data is written
Thin provisioning — if enough volumes fill up simultaneously, the physical storage can run out even though each volume shows free space
Thin provisioning — it makes each individual volume slower than a thick-provisioned one
Thick provisioning — it wastes capacity that could otherwise be used elsewhere
questions.explanation: Allocating more logical capacity than physically exists, on the assumption it won't all be used, is thin provisioning — and its central risk is exactly that: if enough volumes actually use more of their allocation than expected, the underlying physical storage runs out mid-write. Thick provisioning would reserve the full 500 GB per volume up front, which this scenario explicitly isn't doing.

questions.question: A team defines their entire network, VM, and storage configuration in version-controlled template files, and deploys new environments by running those templates rather than clicking through a console. What does this most directly guarantee that manual configuration does not?
options: That the deployed environment requires substantially less patching effort than one configured by hand
That the environment is automatically protected against a full regional outage, regardless of how it's architected
That the same template produces the same, auditable result every time it's deployed
That the environment will automatically scale up or down to match real-time demand
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as Code's core guarantee is repeatable, auditable deployments — the same input produces the same result, and the exact configuration is always readable from the template. It says nothing about patching, autoscaling, or regional redundancy, which are separate concerns configured independently.

questions.question: A team's pipeline automatically builds and tests every code change, and any change that passes all automated tests is released to production immediately with no manual approval step. Which practice does this describe?
options: Continuous integration only, with no release automation
Continuous delivery
A canary release
Continuous deployment
questions.explanation: The detail that removes any ambiguity is 'no manual approval step' — continuous delivery would still keep a human gate before the actual release, while continuous deployment removes that gate entirely so a passing change ships automatically. Continuous integration alone only covers the build/test merge step, not releasing to production.

questions.question: An operations team scripts a workflow that provisions a new VM, installs required software on it, registers it with a load balancer, and then runs a health check — all as one coordinated sequence triggered by a single request. Which best describes what's happening here, beyond just automation of each individual step?
options: Showback
Accounting
Baselining
Orchestration
questions.explanation: Coordinating multiple already-automated steps into a single end-to-end workflow is specifically orchestration — automation alone would only cover one of those steps in isolation, without sequencing them together as a whole.

questions.question: Finance wants each department to see a detailed monthly breakdown of exactly how much cloud spend their team is responsible for, purely for budget visibility — with no actual transfer of funds between department budgets. Which practice fits?
options: A full resource lock on shared accounts
A CMDB entry per department
Chargeback
Showback
questions.explanation: Reporting cost for visibility without moving actual budget between departments is showback. Chargeback would go further and actually bill each department's budget for their share — which this scenario explicitly rules out.

questions.question: A monitoring team wants to know the normal, expected CPU utilization range for a server under typical daily load, observed over several weeks, before deciding what utilization level should trigger an alert. What are they establishing first?
options: A CMDB record
An SLA
A threshold
A baseline
questions.explanation: Observing normal behavior over time to understand the expected range is establishing a baseline. A threshold is the specific trigger value set afterward, usually informed by that baseline — setting a threshold without one first tends to produce either constant false alarms or missed real problems.

questions.question: A provider's SLA guarantees 99.9% uptime for a service. Roughly how much downtime per year does that commitment actually allow?
options: Zero — 99.9% means no downtime is permitted
About 36 hours
About 8.75 hours
About 5 minutes
questions.explanation: 99.9% uptime ('three nines') allows roughly 8.75 hours of downtime per year. 'Five nines' (99.999%) is the tier that only allows about 5 minutes a year — a commonly confused pair on the exam, since both are often just referred to loosely as 'high uptime.'

questions.question: Following the standard troubleshooting methodology, an administrator has identified the problem and formed a theory that a specific firewall rule is blocking traffic. What is the correct next step, before touching any configuration?
options: Document the incident as resolved, since the theory already explains the observed symptoms
Implement a fix by removing the suspected firewall rule immediately, before confirming anything further
Escalate to a change advisory board for approval to test the theory, without doing any hands-on verification first
Test the theory to confirm the firewall rule is actually the cause
questions.explanation: The methodology calls for testing the theory before acting on it — jumping straight to removing a firewall rule based on an unconfirmed theory risks a wasted change (or a new security gap) if the actual cause turns out to be something else entirely.

questions.question: A tenant on a shared virtualization host reports their VM has become sluggish, even though their own workload and configuration haven't changed. Investigation shows another tenant on the same physical host is running an unusually CPU-intensive job. What is this scenario an example of?
options: An orphaned resource
The "noisy neighbor" problem
A licensing failure
A DNS resolution failure
questions.explanation: One tenant's heavy usage degrading another tenant's performance on shared hardware is the textbook noisy neighbor problem. It has nothing to do with licensing, name resolution, or leftover unused resources — the affected tenant's own environment is unchanged.

questions.question: A service is completely unreachable by its hostname, but connecting directly to its known IP address works perfectly. What does this strongly suggest the root cause is?
options: A DNS resolution issue
A firewall blocking all traffic to the service
The service itself has crashed
Insufficient bandwidth to the service
questions.explanation: If the raw IP address works but the hostname doesn't, the network path and the service itself are both clearly fine — the only thing standing between the two is name resolution, pointing squarely at DNS rather than a firewall, an outage, or a bandwidth problem.

questions.question: A hybrid cloud deployment simply means an organization uses two different public cloud providers for two unrelated projects.
questions.explanation: That describes multi-cloud. Hybrid specifically means private and public environments connected and coordinated together, often for workload portability between them — not just using multiple unrelated clouds side by side.

questions.question: A system can be highly available and still experience a brief interruption during a failover event.
questions.explanation: High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy, but a short interruption during failover is often still possible. A system with zero interruption at all, even during a failure, is described as fault tolerant instead.

questions.question: Object storage is generally the best choice for a high-transaction relational database requiring low-latency random reads and writes.
questions.explanation: Block storage is built for that kind of low-latency, random-access workload. Object storage trades that per-operation latency for massive scale and simplicity, and is a poor fit for a live transactional database.

questions.question: An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) can automatically block malicious traffic it identifies, the same way an IPS does.
questions.explanation: An IDS only detects and alerts — it doesn't sit inline or block anything. Only an IPS actively blocks traffic it identifies as malicious.

questions.question: Encrypting a database at rest also protects the data while it is being queried and transmitted to a client application.
questions.explanation: At-rest encryption only protects stored data on disk. Data moving to a client over the network needs its own, separate in-transit encryption (like TLS) to be protected during that trip.

questions.question: A stateless packet filter automatically permits return traffic for a connection it has already approved, without a separate rule.
questions.explanation: That's exactly what a stateful firewall does. A stateless filter evaluates every packet independently with no memory of prior traffic, so both directions of a connection need their own explicit rule.

questions.question: Tokenized data can be mathematically reversed back to its original value by anyone with sufficient computing power, the same as encrypted data with enough time.
questions.explanation: This is the key difference from encryption: a token has no mathematical relationship to the original value at all, so no amount of computing power can reverse it — only looking it up in the separate, secured vault reveals the original.

questions.question: Restoring from an incremental backup chain only requires the most recent incremental backup, the same way a differential backup restore only needs the latest differential.
questions.explanation: An incremental restore needs the original full backup PLUS every incremental backup taken since, applied in order — unlike a differential restore, which only ever needs the full plus the single latest differential, since each differential already contains everything since the last full.

questions.question: A canary deployment exposes a new release to all users simultaneously, the same way a blue-green deployment switches all traffic at once.
questions.explanation: Canary deployments do the opposite — they gradually increase the new release's exposure, starting with a small subset of traffic, specifically to limit the impact of a bad release. Switching everyone over at once is the blue-green pattern.

questions.question: Orchestration can exist without any underlying task automation, purely as a manual coordination process.
questions.explanation: Orchestration specifically means coordinating multiple already-automated tasks into a workflow. Without automated tasks to coordinate in the first place, there's nothing for orchestration to sequence.

questions.question: Chargeback involves actually transferring budget between departments based on their cloud usage, while showback only reports usage for visibility.
questions.explanation: That's the correct distinction — chargeback moves real budget between departments based on their share of usage, while showback stops at reporting for awareness and accountability, without an actual internal transfer of funds.

questions.question: Increasing available bandwidth on a connection will generally resolve a high-latency problem.
questions.explanation: Latency and bandwidth are independent characteristics. Latency is about the delay before data starts moving; bandwidth is about how much can move once it's flowing. More bandwidth does nothing to shorten that initial delay.

questions.question: Applying a quick workaround to restore service during an incident means root cause analysis is no longer necessary.
questions.explanation: A workaround restores service without necessarily fixing the underlying issue. Root cause analysis is still needed afterward, or the same incident is likely to recur.

questions.question: Which two of the following are examples of horizontal scaling, as opposed to vertical scaling? (Choose two.)
options: Adding more replica nodes to a database cluster
Upgrading a VM to a larger instance size with more vCPUs
Adding three more web server instances behind a load balancer
Increasing a single VM's allocated RAM from 8 GB to 32 GB
questions.explanation: Adding more instances or nodes running in parallel is horizontal scaling (scaling out). Increasing the resources of a single existing VM — RAM or vCPUs — is vertical scaling (scaling up), which the last two options both describe.

questions.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish high availability from fault tolerance? (Choose two.)
options: High availability minimizes downtime but may still allow a brief failover interruption
Fault tolerance and high availability are two names for the exact same thing
High availability is only relevant to on-premises systems, not cloud-hosted ones
Fault tolerance keeps a system running through a failure with no interruption at all
questions.explanation: High availability reduces downtime through redundancy but can still involve a short interruption during failover; fault tolerance goes further, with no interruption at all, typically at higher cost. They're related but distinct concepts, and both apply equally to cloud and on-premises systems.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Zero Trust? (Choose two.)
options: It verifies every request independently, regardless of network location
A compromised network perimeter alone is not enough to reach protected resources
It removes the need for authentication once a device is inside the network
It only applies to external users, not internal employees
questions.explanation: Zero Trust verifies every request independently and specifically denies the assumption that being inside the network perimeter implies trust. It doesn't remove authentication for anyone — internal or external — since no request is trusted by default.

questions.question: Which two of the following correctly describe encryption at rest versus in transit? (Choose two.)
options: Encryption in transit protects data moving across a network
Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk
Encryption at rest also automatically protects data once it leaves the server over the network
Encryption in transit removes the need to ever encrypt data at rest
questions.explanation: At-rest and in-transit encryption protect data in two different states — stored, and moving across a network — and neither one substitutes for the other. Data encrypted only at rest is unprotected the moment it starts moving, and vice versa.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Infrastructure as Code (IaC)? (Choose two.)
options: It allows the same environment configuration to be deployed repeatably
It replaces the need for any testing before deployment
It can be version-controlled like application source code
It guarantees an application will never need further code changes
questions.explanation: IaC's real strengths are repeatable, consistent deployments and version-controlled configuration, just like application code. It has no bearing on whether the application itself needs future changes, and it doesn't replace testing — the infrastructure it defines still needs to be validated.

questions.question: Which two of the following are valid reasons a team might choose a rolling deployment over an in-place deployment? (Choose two.)
options: The service needs to remain available throughout the update
It requires maintaining two complete duplicate production environments
Only a few instances are updated at a time, limiting exposure to a bad release
It is the fastest possible way to update every instance simultaneously
questions.explanation: Rolling deployments keep the service available by updating a few instances at a time, which also limits how many instances are affected if something goes wrong. Maintaining two full duplicate environments describes blue-green, not rolling, and updating every instance simultaneously is closer to in-place, not the gradual rolling approach.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about a Service Level Agreement (SLA)? (Choose two.)
options: It typically defines measurable commitments like uptime percentage and response time
SLAs apply only to cloud providers and never to internal IT teams
A 99.9% uptime commitment allows for zero downtime whatsoever
It typically specifies penalties or credits if commitments are not met
questions.explanation: SLAs define measurable commitments (like uptime or response time) and the consequences of missing them. 99.9% uptime still allows roughly 8.75 hours of downtime per year, not zero, and internal IT teams commonly use internal SLAs with their own business units too.

questions.question: Which two of the following correctly describe automation versus orchestration? (Choose two.)
options: Automation and orchestration are interchangeable terms for the same concept
Orchestration coordinates multiple automated tasks into a larger workflow
Automation handles a single, well-defined task without human intervention
Orchestration can be built entirely without any underlying automated tasks
questions.explanation: Automation is scoped to one task; orchestration coordinates several automated tasks together as a workflow, which means it depends on automated tasks existing underneath it — it can't be built purely on its own with nothing automated to coordinate.

questions.question: Which two of the following are steps in the standard troubleshooting methodology, in the correct relative order? (Choose two.)
options: Document findings, before identifying the problem
Establish a theory of probable cause, before testing that theory
Test the theory, before implementing a plan of action
Implement a solution, before establishing any theory of the cause
questions.explanation: The methodology flows: identify the problem, establish a theory, test the theory, then implement a plan of action, verify, and document. Testing must come before implementing a fix, and documentation is the final step, not the first — the other two options both reverse the correct order.

questions.question: A service was recently migrated to a new IP address and its DNS record updated. Some users still reach the old server while others reach the new one. Which two factors most plausibly explain this? (Choose two.)
options: A low TTL was not set before the migration, so cached records at various resolvers have not expired yet
Some users are being served a cached answer from a resolver that has not yet refreshed the record
The service itself is completely down for everyone
The new IP address has no route to the internet at all
questions.explanation: Split behavior right after a DNS change is the classic signature of caching: resolvers that already cached the old record under a long TTL won't re-query until it expires, while others pick up the new record right away. A completely down service or an unreachable new IP would fail for everyone, not just some users.

questions.question: Several VMs on the same virtualization host show consistently high "CPU ready" time in monitoring, even though each VM's own CPU utilization looks moderate. What does this metric specifically indicate?
options: The host's physical CPUs are oversubscribed, so VMs are waiting in queue for CPU time to actually be scheduled
The VMs' guest operating systems all independently developed a memory leak around the same time
The host's storage array is running out of IOPS headroom, and the CPU metric is a red herring
The VMs' NICs are misconfigured for the wrong VLAN, causing retransmissions that look like CPU load
questions.explanation: CPU ready time measures how long a vCPU is ready to run but waiting for the physical scheduler to actually give it time — high ready time across multiple VMs on one host is the signature of CPU oversubscription/contention, not a guest memory leak, a storage bottleneck, or a VLAN misconfiguration, none of which this metric reflects.

questions.question: After a hypervisor host's clock drifts several minutes out of sync, users suddenly can't authenticate to a Kerberos-based service, and TLS certificate validation begins failing intermittently across VMs on that host, even though no configuration changed. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Time synchronization (NTP) drift on the host
A DNS resolution failure
An expired software license
Insufficient bandwidth between the VMs and the authentication server
questions.explanation: Kerberos authentication and TLS certificate validation both depend on closely synchronized clocks — even a few minutes of drift can cause tickets and certificates to be rejected as expired or not-yet-valid. Nothing here points to DNS, licensing, or bandwidth, none of which would produce this specific pattern of authentication and certificate failures tied to a clock issue.

questions.question: New VMs being provisioned in a subnet intermittently fail to come online, with logs showing they never received an IP address. Existing VMs on the same subnet are unaffected. What is the most likely cause?
options: The DHCP scope for that subnet has run out of available addresses
A DNS record for the new VMs is missing
The load balancer's health check is misconfigured
The new VMs' storage volumes are thin-provisioned
questions.explanation: New instances failing to obtain an address while already-running instances (which already hold a lease) are unaffected is the classic sign of a DHCP scope with no addresses left to hand out. It isn't a naming issue at all since the VM never gets an IP to register in the first place, and it has nothing to do with load balancer health checks or how storage is provisioned.

questions.question: In a high-availability cluster, a "split-brain" condition occurs when a network partition causes multiple nodes to each believe they are the only active primary, potentially leading both to accept writes independently.
questions.explanation: That's the standard definition of split-brain — a communication failure between cluster nodes causes more than one node to assume the primary role at once, risking data divergence or corruption if both accept writes. It's why HA clustering typically includes a quorum or fencing mechanism specifically to prevent it.

questions.question: A VM feels sluggish even though its own guest-level CPU and memory metrics look normal. Which two actions would help determine whether the real cause is contention with other tenants on the shared host? (Choose two.)
options: Check hypervisor-level metrics like CPU ready time or memory ballooning for that host
Check whether other VMs on the same physical host are running unusually heavy workloads
Increase the affected VM's own allocated vCPU count without checking anything else
Assume the guest operating system needs to be reinstalled
questions.explanation: Guest-level metrics can look fine while the real bottleneck is contention for the shared host's physical resources — hypervisor-level metrics (CPU ready, ballooning) and checking neighboring VMs' activity are exactly how a noisy-neighbor/contention issue gets confirmed. Adding more vCPUs to a VM that isn't even using its current allocation, or reinstalling its OS, diagnoses nothing and doesn't address host-level contention.

questions.question: Before rolling a critical security patch out to production servers, an operations team first applies it to a staging environment that mirrors production, verifies nothing breaks, and only then schedules the production rollout during an approved maintenance window. What practice does this reflect?
options: Following a formal change management process, validating the change in staging before scheduling it into production
Chargeback, since the cost of the patch rollout is being billed to the requesting department
Orphaned resource cleanup, since the staging environment is being decommissioned afterward
Thin provisioning, since the staging environment reuses overallocated storage capacity
questions.explanation: Testing a change in a representative environment first and deploying it to production only through an approved, scheduled window is the core of change management, reducing the risk of an untested change causing an outage. It has nothing to do with cost allocation (chargeback), unused resources, or how storage is provisioned.

questions.question: By tracking storage utilization baselines over the past year, a team notices consumption has grown steadily by about 10% per quarter and uses that trend to request additional capacity before the array actually fills up. What practice does this describe?
options: Capacity planning based on trend analysis
Chargeback
Root cause analysis
A rolling deployment
questions.explanation: Using historical trend data to forecast future resource needs and provision ahead of time is capacity planning. It's distinct from chargeback (a billing practice), root cause analysis (which investigates incidents after the fact), and rolling deployment (a release strategy) — none of which involve forecasting future demand.

questions.question: A runbook documents a specific, repeatable set of steps for handling a known type of incident, so responders don't have to reinvent the response each time it happens.
questions.explanation: That's the purpose of a runbook — a pre-written, tested procedure for a known scenario, such as restarting a specific failed service or failing over a specific database, which speeds up and standardizes incident response compared to improvising a response from scratch every time.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about a formal change management process? (Choose two.)
options: Even an emergency change made outside the normal approval flow should still be documented afterward
Planned changes are typically reviewed and approved before being implemented in production
Once a change is approved, it never needs to be tested in a non-production environment first
Change management applies only to hardware changes, never to software or configuration changes
questions.explanation: A sound change management process still requires documenting emergency changes after the fact, even when they bypass the usual advance approval, and routine changes are normally reviewed and approved before hitting production. Skipping non-production testing after approval, or limiting the process to hardware only, both defeat the purpose of change management.

questions.question: A development team deploys their application code to a provider's platform, which automatically handles the underlying operating system patching, runtime, and scaling — the team never manages a virtual machine directly. Which cloud service model is this?
options: PaaS (Platform as a Service)
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
SaaS (Software as a Service)
DRaaS (Disaster Recovery as a Service)
questions.explanation: PaaS provides a managed runtime/platform where developers deploy code without managing the underlying OS or VM, which is the defining trait here. IaaS would still require the team to manage the VM/OS itself, SaaS delivers a complete end-user application rather than a platform to build on, and DRaaS is specifically about disaster recovery, not general application hosting.

questions.question: Compared to a traditional virtual machine, what is the main architectural difference that lets a container start in milliseconds and run with a much smaller footprint?
options: A container shares the host operating system's kernel instead of including its own full guest OS
A container typically runs alongside a lightweight virtualization layer that adds negligible overhead compared to a full hypervisor
A container replicates the hypervisor for each instance, providing the same isolation guarantees as a VM
A container packages a full guest OS but strips out unnecessary application dependencies to save space
questions.explanation: Containers package an application and its dependencies but share the host's kernel, avoiding the overhead of booting a full guest OS — that's why they start so much faster and use less memory/disk than a VM, which bundles a complete separate operating system per instance. The other options misdescribe both containers and how virtualization/hypervisors actually work.

questions.question: After a user's password is compromised, an administrator requires that logins also present a time-based one-time code generated by an app on the user's registered phone. Which authentication factor category does this add?
options: Something you have
Something you know
Something you are
Somewhere you are
questions.explanation: A one-time code generated by a registered device the user physically possesses is a "something you have" factor. A password is "something you know," a biometric is "something you are," and location-based checks are "somewhere you are" — combining factors from different categories, rather than just two passwords, is what makes MFA effective against a stolen password alone.

questions.question: A network architecture separates the logic that decides how traffic should be routed (the control plane) from the hardware that actually forwards packets (the data plane), letting routing policy be managed centrally through software instead of configured device-by-device. What is this architecture called?
options: A stateful firewall
Software-defined networking (SDN)
A content delivery network (CDN)
Network address translation (NAT)
questions.explanation: Software-defined networking (SDN) is defined by exactly this separation -- a centralized control plane that programmatically manages routing and policy, decoupled from the data plane hardware that just forwards traffic. A stateful firewall and NAT are specific network functions, not an overall architecture, and a CDN is about caching content near end users, not about how routing decisions are made.

questions.question: A company deploys an appliance in front of its public-facing web application specifically to inspect HTTP requests and block attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting before they reach the application. Which security control is this?
options: A traditional network firewall filtering by port and IP address
An IPS operating purely at the network layer
A web application firewall (WAF)
A VPN concentrator
questions.explanation: A WAF inspects application-layer HTTP traffic specifically for attacks like SQL injection and XSS, which is exactly what's described. A traditional network firewall filtering by port/IP has no visibility into HTTP request content, a purely network-layer IPS is similarly blind to application-layer payloads, and a VPN concentrator terminates encrypted remote-access tunnels rather than inspecting web application traffic.

questions.question: An organization wants its encryption keys generated, stored, and used for cryptographic operations inside dedicated, tamper-resistant hardware, so the raw key material is never exposed to the operating system or application memory. Which solution fits this requirement?
options: A software-based key stored in a configuration file
A stateless packet filter
A content delivery network
A hardware security module (HSM)
questions.explanation: A hardware security module (HSM) is purpose-built dedicated hardware that generates, stores, and performs operations with cryptographic keys internally, so the raw key material never has to leave the device or be exposed in application memory. A key stored in a plain configuration file is exactly the exposure this requirement is trying to avoid, and a packet filter or CDN have nothing to do with protecting key material.

questions.question: A development team ships new code to production behind a configuration switch that starts turned off, then enables that switch for users later, independent of any new code deployment. What does this practice let the team decouple?
options: Deployment (getting new code into production) from release (actually exposing it to users)
Encryption at rest from encryption in transit, since the new code changes how data is protected in production
A full backup from a differential backup, since the deployment schedule determines when each runs in production
Vertical scaling from horizontal scaling, since enabling the switch for users changes how many instances are needed
questions.explanation: This describes feature flags (feature toggles): the code is deployed to production while hidden behind a switch, and enabling it for users later is a separate action entirely -- decoupling when code ships from when it is actually exposed. The other pairings (backup types, scaling types, encryption types) describe entirely unrelated concepts that this scenario has nothing to do with.

questions.question: After reviewing months of utilization data, a team discovers several production VMs are consistently using only about 15% of their allocated vCPUs and memory, and downsizes them to a smaller instance size to cut cost without harming performance. What practice does this describe?
options: Chargeback
A canary deployment
Right-sizing
Orphaned resource cleanup
questions.explanation: Right-sizing is specifically the practice of adjusting allocated resources to match actual observed usage, cutting cost without harming performance. Chargeback is a billing practice, a canary deployment is a release strategy, and orphaned resource cleanup deals with abandoned resources still incurring cost -- none of which describes resizing still-in-use instances to match their real usage.

questions.question: An application repeatedly calling a cloud provider's API begins receiving HTTP 429 responses, and the calls otherwise appear correctly formed with valid credentials. What does this response code most likely indicate?
options: The requested resource does not exist at the endpoint being called
The API is rate-limiting or throttling the client for sending too many requests
The client's credentials have expired and are no longer being accepted
The API server has crashed and is no longer processing any requests
questions.explanation: HTTP 429 ("Too Many Requests") is the standard response code for rate limiting or throttling, telling the client it's exceeding an allowed request rate -- not that anything is wrong with the request's formatting or credentials. A missing resource would return 404, expired credentials would typically return 401, and a crashed server would fail to respond at all rather than returning a well-formed 429.

questions.question: A disaster recovery tabletop exercise involves stakeholders walking through and discussing the DR plan step by step, rather than actually failing services over to a backup site.
questions.explanation: That's the standard definition of a tabletop exercise -- a discussion-based walkthrough used to validate the plan and find gaps without the risk or cost of an actual failover. A full-interruption or live failover test, by contrast, does actually move production traffic to the backup site.

questions.question: A backup job reporting "completed successfully" is sufficient on its own to guarantee the data can actually be restored, without ever needing to perform a test restore.
questions.explanation: A job completing without error only confirms the backup process ran -- it doesn't confirm the resulting backup file is actually usable. Corruption, incomplete captures, and other issues can still make a "successful" backup unrestorable, which is exactly why periodic test restores are considered standard practice rather than optional.

questions.question: Compared to a monolithic application, which two of the following are genuine advantages of a microservices architecture? (Choose two.)
options: Individual services can be updated and deployed independently, without redeploying the entire application
A bug in any one component is guaranteed to never affect the rest of the system
Each service can be scaled independently based on its own specific demand
The entire application always runs as a single deployable unit
questions.explanation: Microservices let teams deploy and scale each service independently, based on that service's own release cycle and load -- both genuine, well-documented advantages. A single deployable unit is a monolithic trait, not a microservices one, and microservices don't guarantee full fault isolation -- a failing dependency can still cascade to services that call it, which is why patterns like circuit breakers exist in the first place.

questions.question: A database VM's queries have become noticeably slower. Which two of the following metrics would most directly help confirm the storage subsystem itself is the bottleneck? (Choose two.)
options: A steady, unremarkable CPU utilization on the same VM
Disk queue length and I/O wait time consistently elevated above baseline
Read/write latency spiking well above its established baseline during the slowdown
A recent increase in successful DNS queries from the VM
questions.explanation: Elevated disk queue length/I/O wait and latency spiking above baseline are direct, storage-specific performance indicators that point at the storage subsystem itself. Steady CPU utilization actually argues against CPU being the bottleneck rather than confirming a storage issue, and DNS query volume has no bearing on storage performance at all.

questions.question: In cloud computing, what does "multitenancy" refer to?
options: Multiple independent customers sharing the same underlying physical infrastructure, logically isolated from one another
A single customer running several separate on-premises data centers
A cloud provider physically dedicating a separate server to each individual customer
A backup strategy that stores copies of data across multiple geographic regions
questions.explanation: Multitenancy is the shared-infrastructure model underlying public cloud economics: many customers' workloads run on the same physical hardware, kept logically isolated from each other rather than each getting dedicated hardware. Dedicating a separate physical server per customer is the opposite (single-tenant) model, and neither a single customer's own multiple data centers nor a multi-region backup strategy describes shared infrastructure between different customers.

questions.question: A team wants to scale a web tier horizontally to absorb traffic spikes, but each user's session data currently lives only in the local memory of whichever server first handled their login. Before adding more servers will actually help spread that load, what has to change first?
options: Session state must be externalized to a shared store (or handled via sticky sessions) so any server can serve any request
The servers must first be vertically scaled to a larger instance size
The load balancer must be removed so each user connects directly to one specific server
The application must be converted from PaaS to IaaS before it can be scaled further
questions.explanation: Adding more servers behind a load balancer doesn't help if a returning user's session data only exists on the one server that first handled them -- new servers just sit idle for that user's traffic unless sessions are moved to a shared external store (or sticky sessions pin each user consistently back to their original server). Resizing the existing servers is vertical scaling, a different axis entirely; removing the load balancer would break routing rather than fix session locality; and the service model (PaaS vs. IaaS) has no bearing on this specific session-affinity problem.

questions.question: What does the principle of least privilege mean when assigning permissions to a user or service account?
options: Granting only the minimum access necessary to perform the required task, and nothing more
Granting the broadest access available up front so the account never needs a future permission change
Granting access based solely on how long the account has existed
Granting the same access to every account in the organization, for consistency
questions.explanation: Least privilege means scoping an account's permissions to exactly what its task requires, minimizing what a compromised account or a mistake could reach. Granting broad access to avoid future requests, basing access on account tenure, or giving every account identical access all work against that goal instead of implementing it.

questions.question: During a TLS handshake, the client and server first use a slower asymmetric key exchange to safely agree on a shared secret, then switch to a much faster algorithm to actually encrypt the bulk of the session's data. Which type of encryption handles that second, bulk-encryption part?
