options: Symmetric encryption, since both sides now hold a common shared secret key
Asymmetric encryption, continued for the rest of the session for stronger security
Hashing, since the data no longer needs to be reversible at that point
Tokenization, since the original data is being substituted with a vault reference
questions.explanation: Once the handshake establishes a shared secret, TLS switches to symmetric encryption for the actual session data because it's dramatically faster than asymmetric operations at scale -- asymmetric encryption is reserved for the initial key exchange, not sustained bulk encryption. Hashing produces a non-reversible digest rather than encrypting data for later retrieval, and tokenization substitutes values via an external vault lookup, which isn't how TLS protects data in transit at all.

questions.question: A security team deploys one tool that passively monitors network traffic and raises an alert when it recognizes a known attack signature, without blocking anything itself. A separate platform then ingests those alerts alongside logs from many other systems, correlating related events into a single case for an analyst to review. Which two tools are being described, in that order?
options: An IDS, then a SIEM
An IPS, then a SIEM
A SIEM, then an IDS
A WAF, then an IPS
questions.explanation: Passively monitoring and alerting without blocking is the defining trait of an IDS, and correlating alerts alongside logs from many other systems into one case is exactly what a SIEM does. An IPS would sit inline and actively block matching traffic rather than just alert, reversing the order would have logs correlated before any alert existed to correlate, and a WAF/IPS pairing describes two different inline-blocking tools rather than a passive detector feeding a correlation platform.

questions.question: A team never patches a running server directly. Instead, any change -- even a minor one -- requires building a brand-new server image with the change baked in and replacing the old running instance entirely. What principle is this following?
options: Immutable infrastructure
Blue-green deployment, applied to a single server instead of a full environment
Thin provisioning
A rolling deployment that patches each instance in place
questions.explanation: Immutable infrastructure means a running instance is never modified after deployment -- any change is rolled out as a brand-new replacement image instead, which is exactly what's described here. Blue-green deployment is about cutting traffic over between two full environments rather than a single-server replacement policy, thin provisioning is a storage allocation technique unrelated to patching approach, and a rolling deployment that patches in place is the direct opposite of never modifying a running instance.

questions.question: After setting a CPU utilization alert threshold based on a solid baseline, the on-call team still gets paged dozens of times a day for brief, harmless spikes that self-resolve within seconds. What adjustment most directly addresses this without raising the threshold so high that a real, sustained problem would go unnoticed?
options: Add a duration (sustained-breach) condition, so the alert only fires once the threshold is exceeded continuously for a defined period
Delete the alert entirely so the team stops getting paged
Lower the threshold further so spikes are caught even earlier
Route every alert to a shared inbox that nobody actively monitors
questions.explanation: A duration or sustained-breach condition is the standard fix for alert fatigue from brief, self-resolving spikes -- it only pages when the threshold stays breached for a meaningful window, while still catching a genuinely sustained problem. Deleting the alert loses real visibility, lowering the threshold further would only page the team more often, and routing alerts to an unmonitored inbox just hides the noise instead of fixing the detection logic.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a CMDB (Configuration Management Database)?
options: To maintain an authoritative inventory of IT assets and the relationships and attributes between them
To store customers' billing and payment information
To run automated remediation scripts against misconfigured resources
To encrypt data at rest across the environment
questions.explanation: A CMDB's job is tracking configuration items -- servers, applications, dependencies -- and how they relate to each other, giving operations and change management an authoritative source of truth about what exists and how it connects. It doesn't handle billing, run remediation itself, or provide encryption; those are separate systems entirely.

questions.question: A user reports that 'the application is slow.' Rather than guessing which layer is at fault, a troubleshooter first checks response time in the browser, then the web server, then the database, then the network, narrowing down at each step exactly where the delay is actually introduced. What troubleshooting approach is this?
options: A top-down approach, systematically narrowing down which layer is responsible
A bottom-up approach, since the network is always checked last in this method
Root cause analysis performed without gathering any information first
A workaround, since no permanent fix is being pursued
questions.explanation: Starting at the layer closest to the user (the application) and moving down toward the network, checking each layer in turn, is a top-down troubleshooting approach -- it isolates which specific layer introduces the delay rather than guessing. A bottom-up approach would start at the network and move up instead, this process is actively gathering evidence at every step rather than skipping straight to a root cause, and nothing here describes a temporary workaround rather than genuine diagnosis.

questions.question: A canary deployment, like a blue-green deployment, requires maintaining two complete, identical production environments at the same time.
questions.explanation: Blue-green deployment is what requires two full duplicate environments with traffic cut over all at once. A canary deployment instead gradually shifts a small slice of traffic to the new version within the existing environment (or a much smaller parallel deployment), without needing a second full production-scale environment standing by.

lessons.title: Cloud Deployment Models & Virtualization
lessons.summary: Public, private, hybrid, and community deployment models, and the virtualization layer underneath them.
lessons.reading:
Cloud deployments come in four flavors, and Cloud+ expects you to reason about the trade-offs independent of any single vendor. Public cloud is infrastructure owned by a third-party provider and shared across many customers — cheapest to start with, since you're spreading the provider's hardware cost across everyone using it. Private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, on-premises or hosted, trading that lower cost for full control and isolation. Hybrid cloud connects both together — usually private infrastructure holding sensitive workloads alongside public cloud handling everything else, with the two coordinated rather than just coexisting. Community cloud is a fifth option that's easy to forget: infrastructure shared by several organizations with a common concern, like compliance, that none of them wants to build alone.

Underneath any of those deployment models, the same IaaS/PaaS/SaaS service-model spectrum still applies — how much of the stack you manage yourself versus how much the provider manages for you doesn't change based on which deployment model you picked. What does change is who owns the hardware and who else, if anyone, shares it with you.

Virtualization is the layer that actually makes any of this possible. A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on physical hardware with no host operating system underneath it — this is what production datacenters and cloud providers run, because removing that extra OS layer cuts overhead and improves performance. A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on top of a regular OS, which is fine for a desktop test environment but not for production at scale. Containers push virtualization a level higher: instead of virtualizing hardware, a container virtualizes at the OS level, sharing the host's kernel across many containers instead of each one carrying its own guest OS the way a VM does — which is exactly why containers start in seconds and have a far smaller footprint, at the cost of being less isolated from each other than separate VMs would be.

As container-based deployments grow past a handful of services, a service mesh often shows up to manage the traffic between them — a dedicated layer, typically sidecar proxies running alongside each service, handling routing, retries, encryption, and observability so individual microservices don't each have to implement that logic themselves.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to cloud deployment models? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of the four deployment models the way you'd think about housing. Public cloud is an apartment building — you get your own unit, but the building, utilities, and staff are shared with every other tenant, and that shared cost is what makes rent affordable. Private cloud is owning a standalone house — nobody else's business happens under your roof, but you're the one paying for and maintaining everything. Hybrid cloud is owning that house while also renting a storage unit across town for the overflow you don't need close at hand, with both places genuinely part of the same plan. Community cloud is a condo association: several homeowners who all care about the same shared concerns — security, upkeep, dues — pooling resources to handle them together, without opening the building to the general public the way an apartment complex would.
commonTraps: Hybrid cloud means private and public environments connected and coordinated together — just running two unrelated clouds side by side for two different projects is multi-cloud, not hybrid.
A container is not just 'a smaller VM' — it shares the host's kernel instead of carrying its own guest OS, which is exactly why it starts faster but is less isolated than a VM.
Type 1 hypervisors run directly on hardware and are the production/cloud-provider standard; Type 2 hypervisors need a host OS underneath them and are typically reserved for desktop or test use.
lessons.scenario: A university, a research lab, and a hospital network in the same city all need to store and process data under the same set of research-compliance rules, but none of them wants to build and maintain that compliant infrastructure alone. Pooling their funding into a shared community cloud, built and governed around exactly those shared requirements, gets all three the compliance posture they need without any one of them owning it outright — and without opening that environment to the general public the way a straightforward public cloud deployment would.

lessons.title: Scaling, Resilience & Storage Patterns
lessons.summary: Vertical vs. horizontal scaling, HA/fault tolerance/DR, RTO/RPO, storage types, load balancing, and RAID.
lessons.reading:
Scalability is the general ability to handle more (or less) load by adding or removing resources — and that can be a manual, planned process, like a scheduled capacity increase ahead of a known event. Elasticity is the specific, automatic version of that: resources scaling up and down dynamically in real time as demand actually changes, with no human approving each step. Within scalability, vertical scaling ("scaling up") means adding more CPU or RAM to an existing instance — simpler conceptually, but capped by the biggest instance size available and usually requiring a restart to apply. Horizontal scaling ("scaling out") means adding more instances running in parallel instead, which avoids that ceiling and that restart, but only works if the workload was actually built to run across multiple instances at once — stateless, and sitting behind a load balancer.

Resilience gets three related but distinct labels. High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy, but still tolerates a brief interruption during a failover. Fault tolerance goes further: the system keeps running through a failure with no interruption at all, usually at a higher cost, because there's no gap for a user to notice. Disaster recovery assumes downtime already happened and covers the plan for restoring service afterward — measured against two targets set by the business first: RTO (Recovery Time Objective), the maximum acceptable time to get back up, and RPO (Recovery Point Objective), the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time since the last good backup or replication.

The building blocks that make scaling and resilience actually work include a few architecture staples: load balancers spread traffic across healthy instances using an algorithm like round robin or least connections, and only ever route to instances that pass their periodic health check — this same idea of a centralized, software-driven control plane deciding how traffic should flow, decoupled from the hardware that just forwards it, is what software-defined networking generalizes across an entire network, not just one load balancer. Choosing the right storage type matters too — block storage for low-latency, random-access workloads like a database's own disk, file storage for a shared, mountable filesystem, and object storage for massive-scale, metadata-rich data accessed over HTTP rather than a mounted drive. RAID adds another layer of resilience at the disk level: RAID 0 stripes for pure speed with zero redundancy, RAID 1 mirrors for redundancy with no capacity gain, RAID 5 adds distributed parity to tolerate one disk failure, and RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping for both redundancy and performance at the cost of half the raw capacity.

None of this is worth much if it's never actually tested. Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures — killing an instance, adding latency, cutting a dependency — into a production or production-like system specifically to confirm that these resilience mechanisms work as designed, instead of discovering the gaps for the first time during a real outage.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to scaling and resilience? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a coffee shop handling a morning rush. Vertical scaling is training your one barista to work faster and adding a second espresso machine at their station — more capacity, but you can only push one person and one station so far before you hit a ceiling. Horizontal scaling is opening a second register with its own barista entirely — no ceiling on how many registers you can add, as long as customers can be routed to whichever one is free, which is exactly the load balancer's job. High availability is having a backup barista who can step in within a minute if the first one has to step away; fault tolerance is having two baristas working the exact same register simultaneously so nobody ever notices a gap at all; and disaster recovery is the plan for what happens if the whole shop has to close for a day and reopen somewhere else.
commonTraps: Vertical scaling hits a hardware ceiling and typically needs a restart to apply; horizontal scaling avoids both, but only for workloads actually designed to run across multiple instances.
High availability can still involve a brief interruption during failover — a system with zero interruption at all is described as fault tolerant, a stricter and more expensive guarantee.
RAID 0 is sometimes mistaken for a resilience feature because it spreads data across disks — it actually has zero fault tolerance and is purely about performance.
RPO is about acceptable data loss, measured in time; RTO is about acceptable downtime. Mixing the two up is one of the most common exam traps in this domain.
lessons.scenario: An online retailer expects a huge, short-lived traffic spike during a single flash sale. Rather than keeping enough servers running year-round to cover that peak, they configure horizontal autoscaling behind a load balancer, so instances get added automatically as real demand climbs and removed again once it falls — true elasticity, not just a fixed schedule. Separately, their order database replicates to object storage backups at a warm DR site sized to meet a 15-minute RPO and a 1-hour RTO, and every quarter the team runs a chaos engineering exercise that kills a production instance on purpose, specifically to confirm the failover actually works before a real outage ever forces the question.

lessons.title: Security Fundamentals: Identity, Encryption & Network Defense
lessons.summary: AAA, access control models, encryption states, Zero Trust, and the network security tools that enforce them.
lessons.reading:
Every access decision on this exam ultimately traces back to AAA: authentication verifies who you are, authorization determines what you're allowed to do once verified, and accounting logs what was actually done, for audit purposes. A stolen-but-valid password is an authentication success and an authorization problem waiting to happen — the credential checks out, but it isn't really that person acting. Two access control models decide the authorization half differently: RBAC grants permissions based on a user's assigned role, simple to administer at scale, while ABAC evaluates a combination of attributes — department, resource tag, time of day, location — dynamically at request time, more flexible but harder to audit since the effective rule set isn't fixed in advance. Single sign-on sits entirely on the authentication side, letting a user log in once and reach multiple systems without proving their identity over and over.

Protecting data means matching the right control to the state that data is actually in. Encryption at rest protects data sitting on disk; encryption in transit protects it moving across a network, like TLS; encryption in use protects data while it's actively being processed in memory, the hardest of the three and typically requiring specialized hardware. A password stolen in transit was never protected by strong at-rest encryption at all — the two controls don't substitute for each other. Tokenization takes a different approach for something like a stored card number: it substitutes the value with a randomly generated token that has no mathematical relationship to the original, with the real data held in a separate vault — unlike encryption, which is always reversible given the right key, a token can't be reversed at all, even with unlimited computing power. Multifactor authentication combines factors from different categories — something you know, something you have, something you are, and sometimes somewhere you are or something you do — and two factors from the same category, like two passwords, still isn't true MFA.

Zero Trust ties all of this together as a philosophy rather than a single tool: no request is trusted just because it came from inside the network perimeter, so a compromised VPN credential or a breached firewall alone still isn't enough to reach sensitive resources, because every subsequent request gets independently re-verified. Enforcing that in practice usually means layered network controls: an IDS monitors and alerts on suspicious traffic without blocking it, while an IPS sits inline and can actively block traffic it identifies as malicious — at the cost of a false positive potentially breaking legitimate traffic, a risk a passive IDS never carries. A stateful firewall tracks a connection's state and automatically allows its return traffic; a stateless filter evaluates every packet independently, with no memory of prior traffic, so it needs explicit rules for both directions of every connection. Segmenting a network into zones — a DMZ holding public-facing servers behind an edge firewall, with a second firewall protecting the internal network behind it — limits how far a breach in one zone can reach.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security concepts? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: This maps closely to airport security. Showing your ID at the gate is authentication — proving who you are. Your boarding pass only getting you onto one specific flight, not any plane on the tarmac, is authorization — what you're allowed to do now that you're verified. The security camera footage of you walking through the terminal is accounting — a record of what actually happened, useful after the fact even if nothing went wrong at the time. Zero Trust is the airport not stopping at the outer perimeter fence: even after you're past the main checkpoint, you still get checked again at the gate, and again if you try to enter a restricted area — being inside one boundary never automatically grants you the next one.
commonTraps: Authentication succeeding — even with a stolen password — doesn't mean authorization or accounting are satisfied too; they're three separate checks.
An IDS only detects and alerts; only an IPS sits inline and actively blocks malicious traffic.
Encrypting data at rest does nothing to protect it once it starts moving across a network — that needs its own, separate in-transit encryption.
A token has no mathematical relationship to the original value at all, unlike encryption, which is always reversible given the right key.
lessons.scenario: A company puts its public-facing web and mail servers in a DMZ, sitting behind an edge firewall facing the internet and a second, internal firewall separating that DMZ from the private LAN — so a compromise of the web server doesn't automatically reach internal systems. Administrators must pass MFA and a device-compliance check before reaching anything, consistent with a Zero Trust posture, and every action they take is logged for later audit. Separately, the payment team tokenizes stored card numbers rather than encrypting them, so that even a full database breach exposes only meaningless substitute values with no way to reverse them back to a real card number.

lessons.title: Deployment Strategies & Migration
lessons.summary: Release strategies, backup types, DR site tiers, migration paths, provisioning, and IaC/CI-CD.
lessons.reading:
Rolling out a new release safely usually comes down to choosing how much exposure a bad version gets before anyone notices. Blue-green deployment keeps two complete, identical production environments; the new version goes to the idle one, gets verified, and then all traffic switches over at once, with the old environment kept running briefly for an instant, all-or-nothing rollback. Canary releases take the opposite approach: the new version reaches a small subset of users or traffic first, with exposure increasing gradually as confidence grows — slower to fully roll out, but limiting the blast radius of anything that goes wrong. A rolling deployment sits in between, updating a few instances at a time behind a load balancer so the service stays available throughout, without the cost of a full duplicate environment.

Protecting the data itself relies on choosing the right backup type. A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind — fast to create, but a restore has to replay every incremental since the last full, in order, and a single corrupted link breaks the chain. A differential backup instead copies everything changed since the last full backup, so a restore only ever needs that full plus the single latest differential. Choosing a disaster recovery site follows the same RTO trade-off: a hot site stays in near real-time sync for near-instant failover at the highest cost, a warm site needs some setup or data sync first, and a cold site has only bare facilities and needs a full rebuild — the tighter the required RTO, the further up that scale you have to pay for.

Moving a workload into the cloud in the first place means picking the migration path that matches where it's starting from: P2V converts a physical server into a VM, V2V moves a VM between hypervisors or platforms, P2C moves a still-physical on-premises workload straight into the cloud, and V2C moves a workload that was already virtualized on-premises into the cloud — a typical "lift and shift" is usually a P2C or V2C migration, moved largely as-is rather than refactored around cloud-native services. Provisioning the storage underneath it involves its own trade-off: thick provisioning reserves the full requested capacity immediately, while thin provisioning allocates space only as data is actually written, letting you over-commit total capacity across volumes — at the risk that if enough thin-provisioned volumes fill up at once, the underlying physical storage can run out even though each one still shows free space.

Once a release process is repeatable, teams typically formalize it with Infrastructure as Code, defining environments in version-controlled configuration instead of manual clicks, and a CI/CD pipeline: continuous integration merges and tests code frequently, continuous delivery keeps it release-ready but still gated by a human approval, and continuous deployment removes that gate entirely so anything that passes automated tests ships straight to production. A feature flag adds one more layer of control on top of any of these: new code can be deployed to production while hidden behind a switch, with actually exposing it to users treated as a separate, later decision.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to release strategies? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of blue-green deployment like a theater that keeps two identical stages built, and simply swings a spotlight from one to the other when the new show is ready — instant, and easy to swing back if something's wrong. Canary is more like a restaurant testing a new dish on a handful of regulars before it goes on the full menu, watching for a bad reaction before serving everyone. A feature flag is like installing a new light fixture in your house but leaving it switched off at the breaker until you're actually ready to use it — the wiring is in place well before the light comes on.
commonTraps: An incremental restore needs the full backup plus every incremental since, in order; a differential restore only ever needs the full plus the single latest differential.
Thin provisioning can let physical storage run out even though every individual volume still shows free space, if enough of them fill up close to their allocation at once.
Continuous delivery still keeps a human approval gate before release; continuous deployment removes that gate entirely.
Deploying code into production and releasing it to users aren't the same event — a feature flag is exactly what lets a team decouple the two.
lessons.scenario: A team migrates an aging physical file server straight into a cloud VM — a P2C migration, moved largely as-is. Once it's running, they define its configuration as Infrastructure as Code so future environments can be rebuilt identically, and set a nightly full backup with hourly differentials sized to meet a tight RPO. New releases to the application in front of that data go out blue-green, with a fresh feature flag left off until support confirms the new version is stable, decoupling the moment the code ships from the moment users actually see it.

lessons.title: Day-to-Day Operations & Governance
lessons.summary: Automation, cost visibility, monitoring baselines, SLAs, change management, and keeping infrastructure documented.
lessons.reading:
Two related terms describe how routine operational work actually gets done. Automation handles one well-defined task without a human doing it by hand, like auto-restarting a failed service. Orchestration coordinates multiple already-automated tasks into a larger workflow — provisioning a VM, then configuring it, then registering it with a load balancer, all as one sequence — and it can only exist on top of tasks that are individually automated already, not as a purely manual coordination process. A runbook is the documented procedure that automation or orchestration actually carries out: a step-by-step set of instructions for a specific task or incident, written so it produces the same result whether a person follows it or a script triggers it.

None of that operational work means much without first knowing what "normal" looks like. A baseline is the expected range of a metric under typical conditions, established by observing it over time; a threshold is the specific value that triggers an alert once crossed. Setting a threshold before establishing a baseline tends to produce either constant false alarms or missed real problems — baselining has to come first. Capacity planning builds directly on that same baseline, using historical trends to forecast future resource needs and provision ahead of demand rather than reacting once something's already exhausted. A Service Level Agreement formalizes uptime and response expectations into measurable commitments — like 99.9% monthly uptime, which still allows roughly 8.75 hours of downtime a year, not zero — backed by penalties or credits if they're missed.

Keeping cost and configuration visible and accountable rounds out day-to-day operations. Chargeback actually bills each department for their share of cloud spend, moving real budget between them; showback reports the same usage and cost for visibility and accountability without that actual transfer, and is often adopted first as the lower-friction option. A configuration management database (CMDB) tracks an organization's IT assets and the relationships between them, so a change or incident process can answer "what else does this affect" instead of relying on institutional memory — which is exactly what a formal change management process is built to protect: proposing, reviewing, approving, and recording a change, including a rollback plan, before it's actually made, with patch management applying that same discipline specifically to software and OS updates inside an approved maintenance window. Immutable infrastructure takes change management a step further by design — servers or containers are never modified after being provisioned, so a change means replacing the instance entirely rather than patching a live system in place, which pairs naturally with Infrastructure as Code.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to day-to-day cloud operations? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A runbook is like a recipe card for one specific dish; automation is the stand mixer doing that one step without you standing there turning a spoon; orchestration is the head chef who reads several recipe cards and coordinates the ovens, the mixer, and the staff so the whole meal comes out together, on time. Baselining is knowing your own resting heart rate before your doctor decides what heart rate should actually worry them — without that normal number first, any alarm threshold is just a guess.
commonTraps: Orchestration can't exist without automated tasks underneath it to coordinate — it isn't a purely manual coordination process.
Setting an alert threshold before establishing a baseline tends to produce either constant false alarms or missed real problems.
Showback only reports usage and cost for visibility; chargeback is the one that actually moves budget between departments.
A 99.9% SLA still allows roughly 8.75 hours of downtime a year — an SLA is a measurable commitment with a financial remedy, not a zero-downtime guarantee.
lessons.scenario: An operations team spends several weeks observing normal CPU and memory behavior across its fleet before setting any alert thresholds, avoiding the false-alarm problem a rushed threshold would have caused. They report departmental cloud spend through showback rather than chargeback, since the organization isn't ready to actually move budget between teams yet. Before a critical patch reaches production, it goes through a formal change management process — tested in staging, scheduled into an approved maintenance window — and because the fleet is treated as immutable infrastructure, that patch actually ships as a freshly built replacement instance rather than a live in-place update, with the CMDB updated the moment the change completes.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Cloud Environments
lessons.summary: The standard troubleshooting methodology and the most common categories of cloud failures.
lessons.reading:
CompTIA's troubleshooting methodology is a fixed sequence, and the exam tests the order as much as the steps themselves: identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test that theory, establish a plan of action and implement the solution, verify full system functionality, and document findings and outcomes. The step most often skipped under pressure is testing the theory — jumping straight from a plausible-sounding cause to a fix risks wasting a maintenance window, or making things worse, if that cause turns out to be wrong.

Two failure patterns show up specifically because cloud infrastructure is shared and elastic in ways on-premises hardware isn't. The "noisy neighbor" problem is one tenant's heavy resource usage degrading another tenant's performance on the same underlying physical hardware, even though the affected tenant's own configuration hasn't changed at all — the fix is usually resource governance or moving the noisy workload elsewhere, not something the affected side can fix on their own. Orphaned resources are disks, snapshots, public IPs, or load balancers left behind after the workload that created them was deleted, quietly still incurring cost — a classic explanation for a bill that's grown even though the deployed footprint clearly hasn't.

Two more failure categories are easy to misdiagnose because everything about the infrastructure itself looks fine. A DNS-related failure happens when the network path and destination service are both healthy but a hostname simply won't resolve correctly — if a service is unreachable by name but reachable by its raw IP, the problem is DNS, not the network path or the service itself. Latency and bandwidth are frequently confused: latency is the delay before data starts moving at all, bandwidth is how much can move once it's flowing, and a connection can have plenty of bandwidth while still feeling slow because of high latency — adding more bandwidth does nothing to fix a latency problem, since they're independent characteristics with different causes.

A quick fix and a real fix aren't the same thing. A workaround, like restarting a hung service, restores service fast without necessarily addressing why it happened in the first place. Root cause analysis is what actually identifies and addresses the underlying reason, to prevent the same incident from quietly repeating — applying a workaround under time pressure isn't the mistake; stopping there and never following up with root cause analysis is.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to structured troubleshooting? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: This methodology maps almost exactly onto how a doctor works through an unfamiliar set of symptoms. They start by identifying the problem — what's actually wrong — then form a theory about the likely cause, and critically, run a test to confirm that theory before prescribing anything, rather than guessing and hoping. Only once the theory checks out do they treat it, then confirm the patient has actually recovered, and finally write it all down in the chart — so the next visit, whether it's the same doctor or someone else entirely, isn't starting from zero.
commonTraps: Jumping straight to implementing a fix without testing the theory first risks wasting a maintenance window on a cause that turns out to be wrong.
More bandwidth does nothing to fix a high-latency problem — the two are independent characteristics with different causes.
A workaround restores service quickly but doesn't necessarily fix the underlying issue — root cause analysis still needs to happen afterward.
If a service is unreachable by hostname but reachable by its raw IP address, the problem is DNS, not the network path or the service itself.
lessons.scenario: A support engineer gets a ticket that one VM feels sluggish. Rather than immediately resizing it, they follow the methodology: they identify the specific symptom, form a theory that another tenant on the same host is consuming excess CPU, and test that theory by checking hypervisor-level CPU ready time and the activity of neighboring VMs before touching anything — confirming a noisy-neighbor problem rather than a fault in the sluggish VM itself. In the same sprint, they trace an unexplained billing increase to a handful of orphaned disks left over from a deleted project, and separately restore a hung reporting service with a quick restart — a workaround they make sure to follow up with a proper root-cause investigation before closing the ticket, rather than treating the restart itself as the fix.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: You have 90 minutes for 90 questions — about 1.0 minutes each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.
Real scoring isn't a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — treat 83%+ as a safe buffer to aim for, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and you get partial credit for nothing by running out of time on one question.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam format & domain weights
points: Up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, scored on a 100-900 scale with 750 required to pass.
Six domains: Cloud Architecture 23%, Deployment 19%, Security 19%, Operations 17%, Troubleshooting 12%, DevOps Fundamentals 10%.
CV0-004 added the DevOps Fundamentals domain that the prior CV0-003 version did not have.

cheatSheet.heading: Service & deployment models (vendor-neutral)
points: IaaS/PaaS/SaaS follow the same responsibility gradient as any vendor's version, but Cloud+ expects you to reason about it independent of any one brand.
Community cloud = shared by several organizations with common concerns (e.g., compliance) — distinct from public (open to anyone) and private (single org).
Multi-cloud = using more than one public cloud provider; hybrid cloud = mixing cloud with on-premises. Don't conflate the two terms.

cheatSheet.heading: High availability & scaling
points: Vertical scaling ("scale up") = a bigger instance; horizontal scaling ("scale out") = more instances — horizontal generally scales further with less downtime.
Active-active = all nodes serve traffic simultaneously; active-passive = a standby node takes over only after a failure.
N+1 redundancy = one spare unit beyond what is needed; N+2 adds two — higher N raises resilience and cost together.
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how long you can tolerate being down; RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable.

cheatSheet.heading: Security domain essentials
points: Encryption in transit (TLS) and encryption at rest (disk/storage-level) are normally both required, not an either/or choice.
Least privilege and role-based access apply the same cloud-agnostic way regardless of which vendor's IAM implements them.
Segmentation (VLANs, subnets, security groups) limits the blast radius of a single compromised host.
Compliance frameworks (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR) drive specific technical controls, not just policy paperwork.

cheatSheet.heading: Deployment concepts
points: Blue-green deployment = two full environments with traffic cut over all at once; canary = a gradual rollout to a subset of users first.
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) makes deployments repeatable and version-controlled versus manual, click-ops provisioning.
Functional, regression, performance/load, and usability testing each answer a different question — know which one a scenario is describing.

cheatSheet.heading: Operations & troubleshooting methodology
points: CompTIA's troubleshooting methodology, in order: identify the problem, establish a theory, test the theory, establish a plan of action, implement the plan, verify full system functionality, document the incident.
Baseline metrics must be captured BEFORE an incident — without one you can't prove current behavior is actually abnormal.
Logging records events, monitoring observes trends over time, and alerting notifies when a threshold is crossed — three distinct layers, not synonyms.

cheatSheet.heading: DevOps fundamentals (the new domain)
points: CI (continuous integration: merge/build/test frequently) feeds CD (continuous delivery/deployment: automated release).
Containers package an app with its dependencies for portability; orchestration manages many containers' lifecycle and scaling.
Version control and automated testing are treated as core DevOps practices on this exam, not optional extras.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: Cloud+ is vendor-neutral — don't answer with a specific AWS/Azure/GCP service name unless the question itself names that provider.
On "which metric confirms the bottleneck" questions, pick the metric that directly measures that resource, not a plausible-sounding but unrelated one.
Real scenarios often touch multiple domains at once (e.g., a control that is both security and HA) — answer based on what the question emphasizes.

madlibs.scenario: A database server is running out of CPU and memory under load, so the team upgrades it to a bigger instance size — this is {b1} scaling. A separate web tier instead handles increased load by adding more identical server instances behind a load balancer — this is {b2} scaling.

options: vertical
horizontal
vertical

madlibs.explanation: Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger single instance; horizontal scaling (scale out) means more instances in parallel — horizontal generally scales further but needs a load balancer and often a stateless design.

madlibs.scenario: Data sitting in a database file on disk is protected using encryption {b1}. That same data, while actively moving across the network between the app server and the database, is instead protected using encryption {b2}.

options: at rest
in transit
in use
at rest
in transit
in use

madlibs.explanation: At rest = stored data (disk, database files); in transit = data actively moving across a network (TLS); in use = data actively being processed in memory (a less commonly tested third state).

madlibs.scenario: A tenant on a shared multi-tenant cloud host notices their VM's disk I/O performance randomly degrades even though their own workload hasn't changed — another tenant on the same physical hardware is consuming a disproportionate share of resources. This is called the {b1} problem, and one common mitigation is moving to {b2} hardware, which reserves the hardware exclusively for one tenant.

options: noisy neighbor
split-brain
orphaned resource
thundering herd
dedicated
shared
burstable
spot

madlibs.explanation: "Noisy neighbor" describes resource contention from other co-located tenants on shared infrastructure. Dedicated (single-tenant) hardware removes that contention entirely, at a higher cost.

madlibs.scenario: A team wants to test a new release with just 5% of production traffic before expanding it further, so they choose a {b1} rollout. Another team instead maintains two complete, identical environments and cuts every user over in one atomic switch, which is a {b2} deployment. A third team can't spare duplicate infrastructure, so it updates only a few servers at a time while the rest keep serving traffic, which is a {b3} deployment.

madlibs.explanation: Canary gradually exposes a new release to a small slice of traffic first, limiting the blast radius of a bad release. Blue-green keeps two full duplicate environments and switches all traffic at once, giving an instant, whole-environment rollback option. Rolling updates a subset of instances at a time within the existing environment -- no duplicate infrastructure needed -- unlike an in-place deployment, which updates everything at once with no gradual exposure at all.
